Generative artificial intelligence, large language models, and agentic
rapid-development environments (such as Lovable, Replit, v0, and Cursor)
are fundamentally transforming research software. Biomedical researchers
increasingly build and publish interactive web applications, analytical
dashboards, clinical decision calculators, and bioinformatics pipelines
created entirely or substantially through AI generation. However, no
standardized reporting guideline exists to disclose how these AI-built
scientific web platforms are constructed, verified, and preserved. Existing
guidelines (such as CONSORT-AI, STARD-AI, or TRIPOD-AI) govern AI
algorithms applied to research datasets, while general AI authorship
checklists (such as CHAT-GUIDE) govern text generation in manuscripts. None
address the reproducibility, computational accuracy, and data security
risks unique to AI-generated software platforms. Unstandardized reporting
in this domain introduces four major scientific vulnerabilities:

1.  Model, Platform, and Prompt Provenance: Papers rarely document the
    underlying foundation model, temperature, platform versions, system
    prompts, or agentic iteration history used to generate the code.

2.  Algorithmic and Mathematical Verification: Generative AI models
    frequently introduce subtle mathematical or statistical hallucinations
    into computational logic. There is currently no reporting checklist
    requiring authors to verify in-browser or backend calculations against
    gold-standard scientific packages (such as R Bioconductor or Python
    SciPy).

3.  Data Governance and Patient Privacy: AI-scaffolded web platforms often
    introduce undocumented third-party telemetry, cloud database syncing,
    or external API calls, creating severe privacy risks when handling
    human or clinical data. Authors must explicitly report whether
    processing occurs entirely client-side or involves remote servers.

4.  Reproducibility and Software Decay: AI web platforms frequently update
    underlying dependencies or deprecate hosting runtimes, causing tools to
    break after publication. Authors must report self-contained source
    repositories, dependency lockfiles, and long-term archival plans (e.g.,
    Zenodo/Software Heritage).

SWAP-AI will establish an international, consensus-based minimum reporting
checklist for any peer-reviewed scientific paper presenting, validating, or
deploying web applications and analytical platforms built with AI-assisted
or agentic workflows.
